rationale: The Dismiss control is a <div id="dismiss"> with an inline onclick that removes the banner, but it has no tabindex (so it is not in the focus order), no role, and no keydown/keyup handler. A keyboard user can neither focus it nor activate it; the action is mouse-only.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints."

rationale: The Apply coupon control is a <span id="apply"> visually styled as a button with an inline onclick, but a span has no native interactive semantics, no tabindex, no role, and no keyboard handler. It is reachable and activatable only by mouse.
citation: Failure F59: "Failure of Success Criterion 4.1.2 due to using script to make div or span a user interface control in HTML without providing a role for the control." (the div/span-as-control pattern that also strands keyboard users).

rationale: The Like control (<div id="like">) is wired with addEventListener('click', ...) only. There is no keydown/keyup/keypress listener, no tabindex, and no role, so the increment fires from mouse click but never from a keyboard interface.
citation: Technique G90: "Providing keyboard-triggered event handlers." SCR20 advises pairing keyboard and mouse event handlers; here only the mouse (click) handler is provided.

rationale: The Reset control (<div id="reset" role="button">) declares the button role and an onclick, but without tabindex it is NOT placed in the keyboard focus order (role alone does not make a non-native element focusable), and there is no key handler. So even though it reads as a button, a keyboard user cannot focus or operate it.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes ..."

rationale: The Follow control (<div id="follow" role="button" tabindex="0">) is focusable, but it only has an onclick handler — there is no keydown handler — so when a keyboard user Tabs to it and presses Enter or Space, nothing happens. Focusable but not activatable by keyboard.
citation: Technique SCR20: provide both keyboard and mouse event handlers. Here the element is focusable but only the mouse (click) handler exists, so Enter/Space do not activate it (2.1.1).

rationale: The Bold toggle (<div id="bold">) binds its only handler to the mousedown event. mousedown is a pointer-specific event that the keyboard never dispatches, and the element has no tabindex, role, or key handler, so the toggle is mouse-only.
citation: Failure F42: "Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, or 2.4.3 due to using scripting events to emulate links in a way that is not programmatically determinable." (mouse-only scripted activation).

rationale: The Chat control is an <a id="chat"> with NO href and only an onclick. An anchor without href is not keyboard-focusable and is not in the tab order, so the scripted activation is reachable only by mouse — the classic scripted-link emulation.
citation: Failure F42: "Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, or 2.4.3 due to using scripting events to emulate links in a way that is not programmatically determinable."

rationale: The entire article card (<div id="card">) navigates via onclick (location.href). The div has no tabindex, no role, and no key handler, so the navigation is mouse-only; a keyboard user cannot reach or trigger the card link.
citation: EN 301 549 clause 9.2.1.1 (maps to WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard): all functionality must be operable through a keyboard interface. A click-only card defeats this.

rationale: The delete control is a glyph-only <span id="del"> with an inline onclick and no text, no tabindex, no role, and no key handler. It is both unfocusable and unnamed; keyboard users cannot operate the delete action at all.
citation: Failure F59: "Failure of Success Criterion 4.1.2 due to using script to make div or span a user interface control in HTML without providing a role for the control."

rationale: The rating star (<div id="star">) activates via onmouseup. mouseup is a pointer-release event that the keyboard never fires, and the element has no tabindex/role/keydown, so rating is mouse-only.
citation: Trusted Tester 5.1 (2.1.1): all interactive elements must be operable by keyboard; a mouse-only event handler (here mouseup) with no keyboard equivalent is a defect.

rationale: The Email-alerts switch (<span id="alerts" role="switch" aria-checked>) flips aria-checked on click only. It has the switch role and an aria state but no tabindex (so it is not focusable) and no keydown handler, so a keyboard user can neither focus nor toggle it.
citation: Technique G90: "Providing keyboard-triggered event handlers." A custom switch must be focusable and toggle on Enter/Space; here only a click handler exists (2.1.1).

rationale: The Next-slide control (<div id="next">) advances on onclick only. A document-level keyup listener exists but it only handles a global Escape (exit) and does not advance the slide, and #next has no tabindex/role/keydown of its own, so the Next action remains mouse-only despite a keyboard listener being present elsewhere.
citation: Failure F42: "Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, or 2.4.3 due to using scripting events to emulate links in a way that is not programmatically determinable."

rationale: The Dismiss control is a native <button id="dismiss"> with onclick. A native button is automatically in the focus order and is activated by Enter and Space by the user agent, so the onclick is reachable by keyboard for free — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): functionality must be "operable through a keyboard interface"; a native <button> satisfies this without scripting.

rationale: The Chat control is an <a id="chat" href="/support/chat"> with an onclick enhancement. Because it has a genuine href it is keyboard-focusable and is activated by Enter; the onclick merely augments the existing keyboard-operable link — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface ..."; an <a> with href is natively keyboard-operable.

rationale: The Calculate control is a native <input id="calc" type="button"> with onclick. As a native form control it is in the tab order and is activated by Enter/Space, so the action is fully keyboard-operable — 2.1.1 met.
citation: EN 301 549 clause 9.2.1.1 (maps to WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard): native interactive controls are operable through the keyboard interface.

rationale: The custom Reset button (<div id="reset" role="button" tabindex="0">) uses the correct ARIA-widget pattern: it is focusable (tabindex=0), declares role=button, and a keydown handler invokes the same activate() on Enter and Space (with preventDefault) as the click handler. Keyboard users can reach and activate it — 2.1.1 met.
citation: Technique SCR20: "Using both keyboard and other device-specific functions." Here both click and keydown (Enter/Space) handlers trigger the same action.

rationale: The Follow control (<div id="follow" role="button" tabindex="0">) has an inline onclick AND an inline onkeydown that performs the identical state change on Enter/Space. The div is focusable and has an equivalent keyboard trigger, so the functionality is keyboard-operable — 2.1.1 met.
citation: Technique G90: "Providing keyboard-triggered event handlers." The onkeydown provides the keyboard equivalent of the onclick.

rationale: The agreement control is a native <input id="agree" type="checkbox"> with a change handler. The native checkbox is focusable and toggled by Space, and the change event fires regardless of input modality, so the handler is fully reachable by keyboard — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): functionality must be operable through a keyboard interface; a native checkbox is toggled by Space without scripting.

rationale: The FAQ disclosure uses native <details>/<summary id="q1">. The summary is natively focusable and toggles the disclosure on Enter/Space with no script at all, so the expand/collapse is keyboard-operable by default — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface ..."; the native <summary> element is keyboard-operable.

rationale: The sort control is a native <select id="sort"> with an onchange handler. A select is focusable and operable with the arrow keys / Enter, and change fires from keyboard selection, so the sort functionality is keyboard-operable — 2.1.1 met.
citation: EN 301 549 clause 9.2.1.1 (maps to WCAG 2.1.1 Keyboard): a native <select> is operable through the keyboard interface.

rationale: The Create-account control is an <a id="start" href="/signup"> visually styled as a button. Despite the button styling it is a real link with an href, so it is in the tab order and activated by Enter — keyboard-operable — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface ..."; an <a href> remains keyboard-operable regardless of CSS styling.

rationale: The Sign-in control is a native <button id="submit" type="submit"> inside a form. It is in the tab order, activated by Enter/Space, and the form also submits on Enter from a field, so the submit action is fully keyboard-operable — 2.1.1 met.
citation: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (Level A): functionality must be "operable through a keyboard interface"; a native submit button satisfies this.

rationale: Although the wrapper <div id="plan"> has a convenience onclick, the actual operable control under test is the native <button id="choose"> inside it. The button is focusable and Enter/Space-activatable, providing a full keyboard path to selecting the plan — 2.1.1 met (the wrapper merely forwards to the button).
citation: Technique SCR20: provide keyboard and mouse functions; here the genuine control is a native <button>, which is keyboard-operable, so the functionality is reachable by keyboard.

rationale: Truth is a FAILURE: the Mark-done control (<div id="t1">) has no inline handler, no role, and no tabindex, and its behavior comes from a document-level delegated click listener with NO matching keydown delegation, so it is mouse-only. But because the activation is attached via event delegation on document (matched by data-action, not bound to the node), a static per-element reader cannot reliably attribute the handler — or confirm the absence of a keyboard path — to #t1, so the runner should abstain.
citation: Failure F42: "Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, or 2.4.3 due to using scripting events to emulate links in a way that is not programmatically determinable." (delegated click-only activation).

rationale: Truth is a PASS: the Red swatch (<div id="red" role="button" tabindex="0">) is focusable and a generic bindActivatable() helper attaches BOTH click and keydown (Enter/Space, with preventDefault) handlers that run the same selection, so it is keyboard-operable. But because the keydown is wired inside a loop using a variable event-type string rather than a literal el.addEventListener('keydown', ...), a static reader may fail to detect the keyboard handler on this node, so the runner should abstain rather than wrongly flag it.
citation: Technique SCR20: "Using both keyboard and other device-specific functions." Both click and keydown (Enter/Space) handlers are bound here, so the control is keyboard-operable even though the binding is indirect.
